Your High School Self

Faculty professional development · 30 minutes, or 35 with the scenarios (20-minute version below) · Led by counseling · Upper School, any subject

Session plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Teachers leave able to spot the moments when their own high school experience, hard or good, colors how they see and treat a student, with three quick questions to ask themselves in the moment, a reminder of where they themselves felt seen, and a private note on the part of their story most likely to color their day.

Materials

  • Index cards, one per teacher (they keep them)
  • The faculty quick reference (last slide), printed or linked

Flow

  1. 4 minOpening: you at sixteen (private, nothing shared)
  2. 6 minThe research: why high school sticks, and how it shows up
  3. 5 minTwo ways it pops out, and what you brought with you
  4. 3 minWhere did you feel seen?
  5. 5 minThe tells, and three questions in the moment
  6. 3 minCloser in age, and any age
  7. 4 minTry it: three teachers (optional)
  8. 3 minJust for you: your card

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Twenty minutes: the opening (2), the research, second slide only (4), two ways it pops out (4), where did you feel seen (2), the tells and three questions (5), your card (3). Skip the scenarios, or hand out the cards for later. Share the faculty quick reference afterward.

Before you present
This is private.

Nobody shares their high school memories in this room unless they want to. The opening and the closing card are for each teacher alone. When you take answers, ask what it was like to go back, never what they saw there.

It's a staff meeting, not therapy.

Colleagues, supervisors and people who write evaluations are in the room. Keep the talk on patterns and moves. If someone starts telling a painful story, thank them warmly and offer to talk afterward.

Some memories are heavy.

For some teachers, high school means bullying, abuse, a death, coming out or not being able to. Say early that if something heavy comes up, that's normal, and that counseling is glad to talk, or a therapist of their own if they'd like one. Don't promise follow-up you can't give.

Not a weapon.

"That's your high school self talking" is a thing you say to yourself. Said to a colleague in the hallway, it's an insult. Name that out loud, with a smile.

Your history is a strength too.

The teacher who was the lonely kid often sees the lonely kid first. The point is noticing when the old feeling is steering, not scrubbing it out.

Students don't need your whole story.

A short, true line ("High school was hard for me too") can help. Your full story puts the student in the position of taking care of you. If you share, keep it brief and bring it back to them.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Your high school isn't theirs.

Different decade, maybe a different country, a different size school, a different income bracket, no phones or all phones. When a student's world doesn't match the one you remember, ask before you assume you know how it feels.

Being the only one.

Teachers who were the only one of something in high school (race, religion, accent, money, body, being out or not) may feel a strong pull toward students in that spot now. That pull can be a gift. Check whether the student wants what you needed back then; they may want something different.

The kids who'd have ignored you.

Many of us still feel a flinch around the confident, popular, athletic or wealthy students. They're teenagers too, and they need adults who see them past the image. Notice if they get less warmth from you.

Students who remind you of a group.

Sometimes it isn't one person from your past; it's a type (the jocks, the rich kids, the kids from the other side of town). That's a short step from a stereotype. Bring it back to the student in front of you.

LGBTQ+ students.

Teachers who weren't safe to be themselves in high school, and teachers whose beliefs were shaped by their own school's culture, can both feel stirred by these students. Either way, the student needs the adult who is here now.

What the research says

Older adults recall more memories, more vivid memories and more important memories from ages 10 to 30 than from any other stretch of life. Their favorite music, books and films also come from those years. It's called the reminiscence bump, and it's one of the most repeated findings in memory research.

Rubin, Rahhal and Poon, Memory & Cognition, 1998

By the time teachers start, they've spent about 13,000 hours watching teachers from a student's seat. Lortie called it an "apprenticeship of observation": much of how we teach comes from how we were taught, and we often don't notice it.

Lortie, Schoolteacher, 1975

Among 291 student teachers and experienced teachers, experienced teachers were more secure in close relationships than those just starting, and elementary teachers more secure than secondary teachers. Riley suggests some people choose teaching partly hoping for a "corrective emotional experience" from students, which leaves them more open to feeling rejected by students. The data are a single snapshot, some groups were small, and the motive is a hypothesis.

Riley, Teaching and Teacher Education, 2009

In 750 student teachers, teachers and principals, student teachers reported the most relationship anxiety and avoidance, and principals the least. Secondary student teachers reported more anger at students during their practicum, and more relationship anxiety predicted more anger. The effect was small and many answers were missing.

Riley, Pastoral Care in Education, 2013 (conference version on ERIC)

Student teachers who had been bullied in school felt more empathy for victims than those who hadn't, but they were no better at spotting bullying or more committed to stopping it.

Kokko and Pörhölä, Teaching and Teacher Education, 2009

In a randomized comparison with 32 elementary teachers, a program where teachers reflected in depth on their relationship with one difficult student raised observed teacher sensitivity and brought more closeness for about half the pairs. Small and early, with young children; nothing like it has been tested with high school teachers.

Spilt, Koomen, Thijs and van der Leij, Attachment & Human Development, 2012

In a randomized trial with 224 teachers in 36 elementary schools, 30 hours of training in mindfulness and emotion regulation (CARE) lowered teacher distress and raised observed emotional support in class. It's the strongest evidence that working on the teacher's inner life shows up in the classroom, but it's elementary and much longer than one talk.

Jennings et al., Journal of Educational Psychology, 2017

Clinicians have a name for an old relationship showing up in a new one: countertransference. Writers on teaching have borrowed the idea for decades. The three questions on the card are adapted from how therapists check themselves in supervision. They are a practice, not a tested classroom program.

Siegel and Hartzell, Parenting from the Inside Out, 2003 · Britzman, The Very Thought of Education, 2009

The reminiscence bump: those years got filed as “this is who I am.”

Slide 4 · Notes

Snapshots, small effects. Clinicians will know it as countertransference.

Slide 5 · Notes

Neither column is a bad teacher. Ask, no hands: which do you lean toward?

Slide 6 · Notes

Lenses, not problems. Most people find two or three, often one from each side.

Slide 7 · Notes

A minute writing, then a few words from anyone who wants. This one is lighter.

Slide 8 · Notes

“How old do I feel?” is usually enough. Adapted from clinical supervision, not tested in classrooms.

Slide 9 · Notes

Newer teachers: school channels, open door, no student group chats or personal follows.
